items.title: AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base
items.headline: AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B: MoE trained from scratch on 17.5T tokens, hybrid Kimi Delta Attention + full attention, Muon
items.summary: Technical report for an 80B-total / ~3B-active mixture-of-experts base model trained from scratch on 17.5T tokens. The architecture interleaves Kimi Delta Attention (a gated delta-rule linear attention) with full-attention layers, uses Attention Residuals, and trains with the Muon optimizer. The report also includes scaling-law experiments and an auxiliary loss on the MoE output.
items.result: Per the abstract: 88.7% pass@8 on IMO-AnswerBench and 82.9% pass@8 on LiveCodeBench v5-v6. On WikiWebFacts / HardMultiQA it reports 86.5% / 67.9%, versus 83.2% / 65.4% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B total, 13B active) and 72.8% / 54.5% for Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base.
items.critique: Details come from the arXiv listing abstract only. The knowledge benchmarks named (WikiWebFacts, HardMultiQA) are not standard and may be in-house; the reasoning numbers are pass@8 with no pass@1 given and no baseline numbers for them in the abstract. Training compute, the share of the 17.5T tokens per language, and ablations isolating KDA, Attention Residuals and the auxiliary MoE loss are not stated in the abstract. Whether weights are released is not stated.

items.title: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2: Understanding and Mitigating Recurrent State Instability
items.headline: Stable GDN-2 fixes exponential state growth in Gated DeltaNet-2; +6.80 RULER-128K average at ~1.6B scale
items.summary: The authors trace long-context training failures of Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) to asymmetric erasure in the delta-rule update, which lets the recurrent state grow exponentially. They replace it with symmetric erasure plus decay-regulated residual writing, and prove an O(sqrt(T)) upper bound on state growth over sequence length T.
items.result: On ~1.6B-parameter models versus GDN-2: +6.80 points on the 128K RULER average in the pure-recurrent setting, and +0.62 points on a nine-task average accuracy in the hybrid (linear + full attention) setting.
items.critique: Details come from the arXiv listing abstract only. Single scale (~1.6B); token budget and training compute not stated. The hybrid-setting gain (0.62 points) is small and no variance across seeds is reported. Baselines are limited to GDN-2 in the abstract; no comparison with other stabilised linear-attention variants (e.g. Mamba-2, Kimi Delta Attention) is mentioned, and throughput impact of the modified update is not given.

items.title: DFly2: Turbocharging Long-Context Speculative Decoding by Sharing the Target's Sparsity
items.headline: DFly2 block-parallel drafter reuses the target's KV cache and sparse-indexer picks; 62-81% higher throughput on 64K sets
items.summary: A block-parallel speculative drafter for sparse-attention target models that keeps no KV cache of its own: it reads the target's KV cache and reuses the target's sparse-attention indexer selections, so drafting cost stays flat as context grows. Evaluated on DS-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and Hy4 flash targets.
items.result: Accepts more tokens per step than DFlash and DSpark trained with the same recipe; the margin over the stronger baseline is 3.9-10.5% on general tasks and 10.0-31.5% on long-context and agentic tasks. At high concurrency on DS-V4.1-Flash, at matched per-user decode speed, throughput is 62% and 81% higher on two 64K-context sets.
items.critique: Details come from the arXiv listing abstract only. Only applicable to targets with a learned sparse indexer (DeepSeek-style sparse attention). Throughput gains are reported for one target model and two 64K sets; hardware, batch sizes and the serving engine are not stated in the abstract. Baselines are trained by the authors on their own recipe, so comparisons with the original DFlash/DSpark releases are not shown.

items.title: FlyingStart: Learned Cross-Token Warm Starts for Fixed-Point Decoding in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
items.headline: FlyingStart warm-starts recurrent-depth decoding from the previous token's state; 14-19% fewer loops on Huginn-0125
items.summary: Recurrent-depth (looped) LMs iterate a shared block to a fixed point for every token. FlyingStart initialises each token's iteration from the previous token's stopping state, passed through a closed-form linear map fitted on the frozen model. The map costs under 5% of one loop iteration and needs no retraining of the model.
items.result: On Huginn-0125 it matches the accuracy of the strongest training-free baseline with 14-19% fewer decoding layers, raises batched throughput by 16-18% in two serving engines, and adds a further 10-14% when stacked on self-speculative decoding.
items.critique: Details come from the arXiv listing abstract only. Evaluated on a single recurrent-depth model (Huginn-0125); generality to other looped architectures is not shown. The 'strongest training-free baseline' is not named in the abstract, and which serving engines and hardware were used is not stated.

items.title: Learning from Recurrence: Internalizing Depth-Induced Preferences in Looped Language Models
items.headline: Retrofitted looped OLMo-2-1B trains its shared block on its own deeper-loop outputs; up to 46.2% mean relative math gain
items.summary: The authors retrofit a pretrained OLMo-2-1B with a shared recurrent block, then train only that block on continuations the model itself generates at greater loop depth ('preference write-back'). No reference answers or correctness filtering are used, so the supervision signal comes purely from running more iterations.
items.result: At target depths the updated models beat a non-recurrent control matched for mid-training data and token budget on all six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with a mean relative accuracy gain of up to 46.2%.
items.critique: Details come from the arXiv listing abstract only. Single 1B base model and math-only evaluation. The headline is a relative gain 'up to' 46.2%, which can be large on low absolute accuracy; absolute numbers and the benchmarks are not named in the abstract. Inference cost of running more loops versus the control is not reported.

items.title: DiCALM: Converting Autoregressive Convolution-Attention Language Models into Discrete Diffusion Language Models
items.headline: DiCALM converts LFM2/LFM2.5 conv-attention hybrids into masked diffusion LMs; up to 1.79x faster than matched AR models
items.summary: Most AR-to-diffusion conversions start from pure Transformers. DiCALM adapts hybrid short-convolution + attention models (Liquid AI's LFM2 and LFM2.5) into masked discrete diffusion language models that can decode multiple tokens in parallel.
items.result: In controlled experiments the converted models perform comparably to LFM2.5-based AR models fine-tuned on the same data, with speedups over them at 350M and 1.2B of over 1.4x on average and up to 1.79x.
items.critique: Details come from the arXiv listing abstract only. Small scales (350M, 1.2B). 'Comparable' quality is not quantified in the abstract, and the speedup is measured against AR models of the same family rather than against speculative decoding or other diffusion LMs. How the convolutions' causality is handled bidirectionally is not described in the abstract.

items.title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents
items.headline: CARE-OPD on-policy distillation for agents reaches 59.5% SWE-bench Verified with 45% less training time than async OPD
items.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) for long-horizon agents is expensive because every update needs fresh environment rollouts. CARE-OPD collects trajectories to expand coverage of interaction histories, gates updates whose teacher signal is unreliable, and allocates hindsight replay of past prefixes based on evidence of usefulness.
items.result: Outperforms online OPD and prior prefix-replay baselines. On SWE-bench Verified it reaches 59.5% task success while cutting end-to-end training time by 45% and environment actions by 44% relative to asynchronous online OPD.
items.critique: Details come from the arXiv listing abstract only. Student and teacher models, and the baseline's SWE-bench score, are not given in the abstract, so the size of the quality gain is unknown. Efficiency is measured against the authors' own asynchronous OPD implementation. Results on other agent benchmarks are not quantified in the abstract.

items.title: Rethinking Knowledge Distillation for Diffusion Language Models
items.headline: Forward-KL distillation fails for diffusion LMs; data-free off-then-on-policy KD gets a 93M student from Dream-7B
items.summary: The authors argue that the standard forward-KL token-level distillation used for AR models fails for masked diffusion LMs, and propose a data-free framework that first distills off-policy and then switches to on-policy distillation on the student's own denoising trajectories.
items.result: On MDLM the student reaches GPT-2-judged perplexity 24.75, below the teacher's 27.04. Distilling Dream-7B into a 93M student lowers Qwen-2.5-judged perplexity from 25.23 (forward-KL baseline) to 19.83, with zero-shot benchmark performance preserved.
items.critique: Details come from the arXiv listing abstract only. Generative perplexity under an external judge model rewards low-entropy text and is a weak quality metric; no diversity/entropy numbers are given in the abstract. A student beating its teacher on this metric is a warning sign rather than proof of quality. Zero-shot results are described only as 'preserved', without numbers.

items.title: Bigger Model or Bigger Table? How Much Backbone a Chorus N-gram Module Replaces
items.headline: Chorus n-gram table study: each added table parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters at 16M-349M scale
items.summary: A scaling-style study of the Chorus n-gram lookup module (an n-gram lookup table added alongside a Transformer backbone). The author trains 16M-349M backbones on 1.34B tokens of pre-1918 Polish and measures how large a plain model each table-augmented model matches, i.e. the exchange rate between table and backbone parameters.
items.result: With tables about the backbone's size, Chorus matches a plain model 1.34x its size at 16M and 1.16-1.20x its size from 107M to 349M; each added table parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters. A separate learning-rate search cuts Chorus's gain at 47M by about a third. Chorus trains slower than a plain model of its own size but faster than a plain model of the same loss.
items.critique: Details come from the arXiv listing abstract only. Single author, small scale (≤349M) and a narrow, low-resource corpus of 1.34B tokens, so transfer to modern pretraining regimes is uncertain. The finding that LR tuning removes a third of the gain suggests other reported gains may also partly reflect baseline under-tuning. A useful negative-leaning calibration point rather than a strong positive result.

items.title: LogToPersona: New Benchmark and Efficient Persona Prediction through Semantic Log Filtering
items.headline: LogToPersona filters on-device mobile logs before prompting; up to 39% less memory, 2.5GB saved for Qwen3-4B
items.summary: A day of mobile usage logs is about 30K tokens, whose KV cache alone exceeds the INT4 weights of a 4B model. The paper introduces a persona-prediction benchmark and a semantic filter that keeps only behaviourally distinct log entries before they reach the on-device LM, reducing context length rather than changing the model.
items.result: Across nine models from four families the filter cuts memory footprint by up to 39% and more than halves prefill time; for Qwen3-4B it removes 2.5GB, while maintaining or improving prediction quality.
items.critique: Details come from the arXiv listing abstract only. This is input pruning for one application, not a general KV-cache method, hence marked off focus. The benchmark is introduced by the same authors; no comparison with generic KV-cache compression or eviction methods is mentioned in the abstract.

items.title: When Rerankers Work Together: Better and Faster Reranking without Joint Training
items.headline: Cache-based coarse scorers before CrossEncoder/Provence add 4.02-9.43 points on NoLiMa 32K and speed pruning 1.57-1.88x
items.summary: Proposes Cache-Pointwise and Cache-Shapley, coarse relevance scorers that reuse the reader model's cached computation, placed in front of existing rerankers or context pruners (CrossEncoder, Provence) in RAG pipelines, without training the components jointly.
items.result: With Gemma on NoLiMa at 32K, answer accuracy improves by 4.02-9.43 percentage points while online pruning is 1.57-1.88x faster. Cache-Pointwise fused with ColBERTv2 via reciprocal rank fusion gains 4.60 points at 1.36x speedup over ColBERTv2.
items.critique: Details come from the arXiv listing abstract only. Retrieval-pipeline work, off the architecture/efficiency focus. Results centre on one long-context benchmark (NoLiMa 32K) and one reader family (Gemma); how 'Cache' scorers obtain their cache and its memory cost are not described in the abstract.
